title: Directly Optimizing Natural Language Explanations for Behavioral Faithfulness: Simulatability and Recoverability
claim: A policy trained with RL on faithfulness rewards from multiple classifiers produces explanations that transfer to unseen tasks and human users.
layout: 2 stacked panels split by dashed line, left-to-right flow, red GRPO feedback loop
description: Two horizontal panels are separated by a dashed line. The top panel, in red text, is multi-task training. Stacked blue cards of labeled samples from a classifier (green input samples, red predicted labels) feed an arrow into a large purple OPeX box, 'Optimized Policy for eXplanations'. A second arrow leads from OPeX to stacked pink cards holding a sample explanation. A curved arrow carries the explanation to a gray REWARDS box with a human–neural-network icon and dashed boxes labeled Simulatability and Recoverability. A red 'GRPO Updates' arrow loops from the rewards box back to OPeX. The bottom panel, in blue text, is evaluation on unseen tasks and classifiers. Yellow-background samples feed OPeX, which outputs a wine-classification explanation. A blue 'User Study' arrow leads to purple and blue people icons. The eye goes first to the large OPeX boxes.
caption: OPEX is a natural-language explainer that produces faithful and simulatable explanations of a model’s decision rationale.
abstract: Natural-language explanations are widely used to interpret machine learning models, yet many prioritize human plausibility over accurately reflecting or predicting model behavior. Prior approaches often rely on human-written rationales, producing post-hoc explanations that neither align with the model’s decision function nor generalize. We introduce $\textbf{OPeX}$, a natural-language explanation model that directly optimizes for behavioral faithfulness: the ability of an explanation to reflect and predict a model’s observable input–output behavior. $\textbf{OPeX}$ is trained using reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), optimizing two complementary metrics: recoverability, which measures whether explanations recover model predictions on seen examples, and simulatability, which measures prediction of model behavior on unseen inputs. Across structured and text-based tasks, $\textbf{OPeX}$ achieves high simulatability (∼0.85) and recoverability (∼0.99), outperforming GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.3-70B, MaNtLE, Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-based models, and human-written explanations, despite using an 8B-parameter backbone. Human user studies show a 15% improvement in classification accuracy over competent baselines.
